title: The Hidden Job Market: Why Your Network Finds Jobs Before Job Boards Do
excerpt: Many roles are filled through referrals and quiet conversations before they ever reach a job board. This is the story of how the hidden job market works, and how to build a network that hears about openings first without feeling fake.
content:
Ngozi is a composite of several young professionals we have mentored at Novola, but every piece of her story happened to someone real. At 26 she was an audit associate in Lagos, good at her job and quietly bored by it. She wanted to move into financial analysis at a fintech. So she did what we are all taught to do: polished her CV and started applying on the job boards. Seventy four applications in five months. Two first round interviews. Zero offers.

The worst part was not the rejection. It was the silence. Most applications vanished into a portal and were never heard from again.

Then one evening, in her university alumni WhatsApp group, a man named Tunde posted that his fintech was quietly looking for an analyst who understood reconciliations. Ngozi had spoken to Tunde perhaps twice in her life. She almost scrolled past. Instead she messaged him asking, not for the job, but for twenty minutes to understand what the team actually needed.

That call changed everything. Tunde walked her through the role, told her which skills the hiring manager cared about, then offered, unprompted, to forward her CV with a personal note. Three weeks later she had an offer. The role was never advertised anywhere. It went from an idea in a manager's head to a signed contract without touching a job board.

The market you cannot see

Recruiters call this the hidden job market: the layer of roles filled through referrals, internal moves, and quiet conversations before an advert is ever written. Hiring through people you trust is faster, cheaper, and less risky, so employers do it whenever they can. Hiring data reported by the Society for Human Resource Management, drawn from more than 1,000 companies and over 300,000 hires, found that employee referrals produced about 30 percent of all hires, their single biggest source of new staff.

Now add the African context. The International Labour Organization estimates that 85.8 percent of employment in Africa is informal, the highest share of any region in the world. That tells you how work is actually found on this continent: through people, not portals. Even formal employers in Lagos, Nairobi, and Johannesburg often ask their staff for names before paying to advertise. If you only search where jobs are posted, you are fishing in the smallest pond.

Why acquaintances matter more than best friends

Here is the counterintuitive part. The person most likely to lead you to your next job is probably not your closest friend. In 1973 the sociologist Mark Granovetter argued that close friends move in the same circles you do, so they mostly know about the same opportunities you already know about. Acquaintances, the people he called weak ties, act as bridges into networks you cannot see.

For decades that was theory. Then it was tested at enormous scale. Researchers from MIT, Harvard, Stanford, and LinkedIn ran a five year set of experiments involving 20 million LinkedIn users, during which 600,000 new jobs were created. The results vindicated Granovetter: moderately weak ties increased job mobility more than strong ones, and the effect was even bigger in digital industries. One analysis of the study found that moderately weak ties were more than twice as effective as strong ties at helping a job seeker join a new employer.

Tunde was a textbook weak tie: same university, different year, almost no interaction. His world barely overlapped with Ngozi's, which is exactly why he knew about a job she did not.

Networking without feeling fake

Many young professionals still resist, because networking sounds like begging with extra steps. If it feels fake, you are probably doing the transactional version: appearing only when you need something. The version that works rests on three habits.

Ask for advice, not a job

The informational interview is the most underused tool in African job searching. You ask someone doing work you admire for 15 to 20 minutes, to learn how they got there and what their industry actually rewards. You are not asking to be hired, so there is no pressure on either side. Do your homework first, bring specific questions, and send a thank you afterwards. Let help be offered rather than extracted. When a role opens on their team months later, your name surfaces.

Give before you ask

Generosity is the difference between a contact and a relationship. Congratulate people on new roles. Send someone an article relevant to a problem they mentioned. Forward an opening that suits a classmate. If you are a student, volunteer to help run your department association's events, because the organizing committee meets every guest speaker. It builds a reputation as someone who adds value, and reciprocity does the rest.

Work the communities you already belong to

You belong to more networks than you realize: your university alumni association, your NYSC cohort if you are Nigerian, professional bodies and their student chapters, tech meetups, church and mosque communities. Alumni networks are especially powerful because shared identity lowers the barrier to a cold message. The group you have muted is exactly where Ngozi found her job.

What to actually say

The hardest part is the first message, so here are openers that feel human rather than scripted:

  • "I read your post about switching from audit to product, and it changed how I am thinking about my own move. Thank you for writing it."
  • "I am an audit associate exploring a move into financial analysis. Could I ask you three specific questions about how you made a similar switch?"
  • "We attended the same university a few years apart. I would value 15 minutes to hear how your industry looks from the inside."
  • "I saw your team is hiring for a role I am not ready for yet. I would love to understand what separates a good candidate from a great one, so I can close the gap."

None of these ask for a job. They ask for perspective, which people give far more freely. How you carry the conversation matters as much as starting it, and we cover that craft in our guide to communicating so people listen.

A weekly routine that compounds

Networking fails when it is treated as an emergency measure, started the week after a job is lost. Treat it like exercise instead, small and consistent:

  • Message one weak tie a week: an old classmate, a former colleague. No agenda, just a genuine check in.
  • Leave two thoughtful comments on posts from people in your target industry. Quiet visibility compounds.
  • Request one informational interview every two weeks, and prepare three specific questions for each.
  • Share one useful thing a week: an article, an opening that suits someone else, an introduction.
  • Attend one gathering a month, whether an alumni meetup in Accra or a developer meetup in Nairobi.
  • Keep a simple tracker of who you met, what you discussed, and when to follow up.

An hour a week is enough. Six months of this puts you inside conversations job boards will never show you.

Be somebody's Tunde

None of this replaces competence. When the referral lands, you still need a CV that survives scrutiny and you still need to perform in the interview room. It also helps to point your network at sectors that are actually expanding, which we map in our guide to where the jobs are across Africa. But competence that nobody knows about is a well with no bucket.

A year into her new role, Ngozi posted in the same alumni group that her team was hiring, before the advert went live. Three graduates messaged her. One now sits two desks away. The hidden job market never disappears. The only question is whether you are standing inside it, or waiting outside refreshing a job board.
